Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

I had played piano a little as a child, but the cello felt completely different. The case was taller than my kitchen chair, and the first time I opened it I could smell the varnish and the old wool cloth tucked around the bridge. My teacher was Mr. Chen, and he had a quiet voice and a habit of tapping the pencil against his music stand when he was thinking.

Our first lesson was on a Thursday afternoon after a heavy rain. The hallway smelled like wet coats, and the room had two narrow windows facing the bus stop. Mr. Chen showed me how to loosen the bow and how to tighten it before playing. He said, “Not too much, or the hair would be under stress.” Then he asked me to sit on the front half of the chair and let the cello rest against my chest. I kept moving the endpin because it seemed either too high or too low. He said, “Let the instrument find a comfortable place rather than chasing a perfect position.” I remember that because it made the whole lesson feel less like a test.

I would stop every few seconds to look at my right hand, and then the sound would get worse. At home, I practiced in the spare room with a towel under the endpin because the floor was slippery. The upstairs neighbor once knocked on the ceiling, and Elena told me later that it was probably the washing machine, not my playing. I was relieved, but I still shut the window before practicing.

The routine that helped me most was putting the music stand near the bookcase, checking the chair and endpin before I picked up the bow, tuning with the small electronic tuner, and playing each open string twice. I kept a notebook on the piano and wrote down the part that had felt difficult. The teacher had suggested ten focused minutes rather than an hour of repeating mistakes, so I used a kitchen timer. When it rang, I often wanted to keep going, but I stopped if my shoulder was tight. One week I wrote that the A string sounded like a door hinge, and the next week I could hear a clear note for almost four seconds. That small change felt bigger than learning a whole song.

Mr. Chen taught me a short folk melody called “The Sailor’s Return,” and we worked on it one measure at a time. The first time I played the whole thing, I skipped the second line and ended on a note that was not in the tune. I laughed and said, “Well, that sounded like a different sailor.” Mr. Chen smiled and said, “Maybe he took a different boat.” He did not make me start again right away. He asked me to sing the melody first and tap the rhythm on my knee. Then we marked two places in the sheet music where I needed to shift my left hand. I had thought the fingers were supposed to press hard, but he showed me that a light touch could still make the note speak.

In November, the library hosted a small student afternoon in the meeting room, and I agreed to play the melody for Elena and two other students. It was not a formal concert, but I was nervous anyway. The room had folding chairs and a paper sign on the door that said, “Please keep the corridor clear.” I arrived early with the cello in its case and checked the tuning beside a radiator, which kept clicking as it warmed up. My hands were cold, and I started the first phrase too quickly. Mr. Chen gave me a small nod, and I slowed down after the first two notes. I forgot one change in the melody, but I stayed with the rhythm and finished the tune. Nobody clapped loudly because there were only a few people, but Elena said she could finally hear the sailor coming back into the harbor.

By the end of the semester, I could tune the strings with less help and move the bow across them without watching every inch of it. I still had trouble keeping my left thumb loose, and I sometimes raised my shoulder when a passage became difficult. Mr. Chen noticed that during the final lesson and asked me to pause instead of pushing through. He said, “The pause was part of the practice too.” I had thought progress meant playing a longer piece each week, but I started to understand that it could mean hearing one note more clearly or noticing tension before it turned into pain.

I gave the cello back to Elena in January after she needed it for her daughter again. Before returning it, I wiped the rosin dust off the strings with a soft cloth and put the spare pencil and my notebook in the side pocket. I felt sad to close the case, but I did not feel finished with lessons. I asked Mr. Chen if beginners ever rented instruments month by month, and he said the music shop on Maple Street had a few student cellos. He wrote down the shop hours on the back of an old recital flyer. I went there the following Saturday and rented a smaller cello for another term.
